name: Betaine

lead: Betaine, also called trimethylglycine, is a small compound found in beets, spinach, wheat and shellfish. It is also produced in the body from choline and sold as a supplement for sports use.

Studies have looked at strength, power and body composition. A meta-analysis suggests a small gain in maximal strength, mainly lower body, while evidence for body composition and power is inconsistent.

paras: Betaine acts as an osmolyte that protects cells under stress and as a methyl donor, converting homocysteine to methionine. Proposed performance effects include better cell hydration, creatine synthesis support and effects on anabolic signalling, though human data are limited.

Betaine is legal and has low acute toxicity. Gastrointestinal upset and a fishy odor can occur, and it may raise cholesterol in some people. It is a prescription medicine for homocystinuria; betaine hydrochloride sold for digestion is a different product. Published trials are small and short.

lead: Betaine, also called trimethylglycine (TMG) or glycine betaine, is a small N-trimethylated amino acid derivative first isolated from sugar beets, after which it is named [1][2]. It occurs in beets, spinach, quinoa, wheat and seafood, is made in the body from choline, and acts both as a methyl donor in one-carbon metabolism and as an osmolyte that protects cells under stress [1][2].

As a sports supplement, betaine anhydrous is taken by lifters in the hope of improving strength, power and body composition; it appears in pre-workout powders and is marketed with claims about cell hydration, cortisol and recovery [3][4][5].

Human trials on exercise performance are small and short, with some reporting benefits and others reporting none [6][7][8]. A separate pharmaceutical betaine is prescribed for homocystinuria [2]. The term 'betaine' also covers a chemical class, and betaine hydrochloride sold for digestion is a different product [1].

paras: Betaine anhydrous is taken for strength and power training and sometimes for body composition. T Nation's pre-workout products list 2 to 2.5 g servings alongside citrulline malate and beta-alanine [3][4][5][9]. The site's descriptions say betaine promotes intracellular hydration and cell volumisation and reduces cortisol to mitigate overtraining stress [5][10]. Forum users list it among pre-workout ingredients in training logs [11].

Betaine is a prescription medicine for homocystinuria, a genetic disorder of methionine metabolism, according to Grokipedia [2]. A registered trial studied betaine metabolism in homocystinuria (NCT02404337) [12]. Other trials have examined betaine in peroxisome biogenesis disorders, steatohepatitis, lipid metabolism in overweight women and in lactating mothers [13][14][15][16][17]. Cosmetic products use betaine as a humectant and skin conditioner, and cocamidopropyl betaine derivatives are surfactants in shampoos [1][2].

A 2010 review in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition discussed ergogenic effects of betaine on strength and power [18]. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis examined chronic betaine supplementation and exercise performance [6]. A 2020 trial reported that betaine did not improve muscle hypertrophy or strength after six weeks of CrossFit training [7]. A 2025 randomised trial in cyclists reported that betaine improved 60 km time-trial performance and one-carbon metabolism during recovery [8]. Registered trials include betaine with blood flow restriction training (NCT05790070), exercise and gut permeability (NCT06392360) and firefighter thermoregulation (NCT06042270) [19][20][21].

Grokipedia reports low toxicity, a generally recognised as safe classification for food use, and rapid absorption with peak plasma levels within about an hour [2]. An observational literature links gut-microbe metabolism of choline-containing compounds to trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO) and cardiovascular risk [22][23]; a trial examined TMAO in vegetarians [24]. These studies concern choline pathways and are not direct tests of betaine supplements.

Betaine donates a methyl group to convert homocysteine to methionine through betaine-homocysteine S-methyltransferase, and is an osmoprotectant that stabilises proteins and cell structures under osmotic stress [2][25]. Proposed performance mechanisms include cell hydration, support for creatine synthesis and anabolic signalling; the sources cited do not show these mechanisms in healthy trainees. Betaine has also been studied in inflammation research [26] and in nutrition and epigenetics reviews [27].

Betaine was first isolated in 1869 from sugar beet molasses by Hermann Scheibler, according to Grokipedia, which also dates the elucidation of its methyl-donor role to the 1940s and its osmoprotectant role in bacteria to the 1960s [2]; these dates come from an AI-generated source and were not independently verified. Wikipedia notes that historically the term was reserved for trimethylglycine [1].
Exercise: a 2010 review [18], a 2024 meta-analysis [6], a six-week CrossFit trial [7] and a 2025 cycling trial [8], with registered trials listed above [19][20][21].
Other conditions: registered trials in homocystinuria, peroxisome disorders, steatohepatitis and lipid metabolism [12][13][14][15][17].

lore.intro: Betaine appears on T Nation almost entirely as an ingredient in the site's own pre-workouts and in training logs; discussion of betaine HCl for digestion is a separate topic [3][4][11][28].
